summary: Describes a signaling method and protocol for RSVP-based admission control on IEEE 802-style local networks, such as Ethernet. It lets a device on the LAN decide whether enough bandwidth is available before reserving it. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: A school bus can only hold so many kids. This lets a local network check that there are enough seats for a new traffic stream before saying yes.

questions: what is a subnet bandwidth manager
how does rsvp work on ethernet lans
subtitle: How RSVP reservations are policed on shared and switched LAN segments by electing a bandwidth manager for each segment.

tldr.problem: RSVP lets hosts reserve resources, but a LAN full of Ethernet-style segments and switches has no way to say yes or no to a bandwidth request before traffic starts flowing.
tldr.mechanism: Each managed LAN segment gets a Designated Subnet Bandwidth Manager (DSBM), elected by a small protocol. Hosts and routers send RSVP PATH messages through it, so it sees every reservation and can refuse one with RESV_ERR.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines the roles, the forwarding rules, the election and the new RSVP objects, but leaves the actual admission control algorithm and configuration method open. It is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 2814 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata for this RFC lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It works together with the framework in RFC 2816 and the service mappings in RFC 2815.

sections.title: Goals and Assumptions
sections.content:
RSVP and the Integrated Services service classes (RFC 1633, RFC 2205, RFC 2210) are largely independent of the network technology underneath, so each link technology needs its own mapping. SBM (Subnet Bandwidth Manager) is that mapping for IEEE 802-style LANs. It describes how RSVP-enabled hosts, routers and link layer devices such as switches and bridges cooperate to reserve LAN resources.

The RFC specifies only a signaling method and protocol. It defines no traffic control mechanisms of its own, and expects Layer 3 end systems to police each flow so that it stays inside the traffic specification given in its reservation request. It assumes LANs will stay a mix of legacy shared segments and newer IEEE 802.1p switched segments, so the protocol covers both.

On a plain shared segment with no traffic separation, SBM can only cap the total load from RSVP flows. The RFC argues this is still useful: it keeps that load within the limit the administrator wants, and best-effort TCP/IP traffic is generally rate adaptive. It admits that this does not guarantee other traffic will not interfere.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule book for sharing a classroom pencil box: it does not make more pencils, it just keeps track of who asked for one. It works for old classrooms and new ones.

sections.title: SBM, DSBM and Managed Segments
sections.content:
A segment is a Layer 2 physical segment shared by one or more senders, for example a shared Ethernet wire, a half duplex link, or one direction of a full-duplex switched link. An SBM is a protocol entity in a Layer 2 or Layer 3 device that is able to manage resources on a segment. When several SBMs share a segment, one is elected the Designated SBM (DSBM). At most one DSBM exists for each segment, and its presence makes the segment a managed segment.

Layer 3 hosts and routers that send reserved traffic onto a managed segment are DSBM clients. DSBM clients always sit in Layer 3 devices, and a Layer 2 device never hosts one. A device that knows nothing of SBM is SBM transparent. It passes SBM messages through, so segments joined by transparent devices are treated as one managed segment. The administrator should then configure the DSBM with some reasonable approximation of that combined capacity: a conservative policy uses the lowest-capacity route, a liberal one the highest.

SBMs that are not DSBMs still matter. They stay passive for fault tolerance and step in if the DSBM fails. They also divide the election scope, so that a switch with an SBM gives each attached segment its own DSBM and a simple topology.

The RFC says the efficiency of resource allocation improves as managed segments get smaller. In the ultimate configuration each physical segment has its own DSBM.
sections.plainLanguage: Each hallway has one hall monitor, chosen from the grown-ups standing there. Grown-ups who were not chosen wait quietly and take over if the monitor leaves.

sections.title: How Admission Control Works
sections.content:
The DSBM is configured with limits on the fraction of each segment's resources, such as bandwidth, that may be reserved. The RFC does not specify the configuration mechanism. A DSBM client then follows the basic procedure:

  • When it sends or forwards an RSVP PATH message onto a managed segment, it sends it to the segment's DSBM instead of to the session destination. The DSBM builds PATH state, remembers the previous hop, writes its own addresses into the hop objects and forwards the message on.
  • A receiver replies with a RESV message to the previous hop address from the PATH, which is the DSBM.
  • The DSBM checks the request against the bandwidth available. If it cannot be granted, the DSBM returns RESV_ERR to the requester. Otherwise it forwards the RESV toward the previous hops and merges requests for the same session as ordinary RSVP does.

Because the DSBM inserts itself as a hop, all RSVP messages for the flow (PATH, PATH_TEAR, RESV, RESV_CONF, RESV_TEAR and RESV_ERR) pass through it. This document does not specify the admission control algorithm. It may be fine-grained per flow, coarse and based only on traffic class with a static capacity split, or a mix.

Senders that bypass the protocol are a problem. All senders putting RSVP traffic onto a managed segment MUST be SBM-aware, and DSBMs, SBMs and clients must not accept PATH messages from senders that are not. The RFC also says SBM does not try to solve non-RSVP reservation schemes such as SNMP configuration, though it can coexist with them if resources are partitioned statically or arbitrated by a common allocator.
sections.plainLanguage: Before anyone gets on the ride, they ask the ride operator, who checks if there is room. If the ride is full, the operator says no, and everyone who asks later has to go through the operator too.

sections.title: Addresses and Forwarding Rules
sections.content:
Layer 2 switches should not need to snoop for RSVP or run ARP. So the RFC adds Layer 2 information to PATH messages. RSVP_HOP_L2 carries the MAC address of the previous hop. LAN_NHOP carries both the IP address and the MAC address of the next Layer 3 hop, so a switch can forward by its normal filtering database. Layer 3 devices get the MAC address from a map_addr() function, whose implementation (an ARP cache lookup or an ARP exchange) is left open.

PATH messages on a managed segment use two reserved multicast addresses, so a Layer 2 device can capture them with a static entry. 224.0.0.16 is the DSBMLogicalAddress. SBMs and DSBM clients send PATH messages there, and the DSBM listens on it. 224.0.0.17 is the AllSBMAddress. The DSBM sends PATH messages there, and all SBMs use it for election traffic. RESV messages stay unicast to the stored previous hop. SBM messages use raw IP encapsulation only, so an RSVP node that can only use UDP encapsulation cannot interoperate with the DSBM unless the DSBM also accepts UDP.

When a Layer 3 device sends a PATH onto a managed segment it adds the LAN_NHOP, LAN_LOOPBACK and RSVP_HOP_L2 objects. Leaving the managed domain, it strips them. A DSBM may even send a PATH back out of the interface it arrived on, for example when the next hop is on the same segment, using the AllSBMAddress. To stop such reflected multicast messages from looping, every SBM entity except a reflecting DSBM overwrites LAN_LOOPBACK with its own interface address, and discards any PATH that carries its own address there.

The RFC walks through a sample network (Figure 2) with unicast and multicast sessions to show each device rewriting these fields.
sections.plainLanguage: A letter needs both a street address and the name on the mailbox so the mail room does not have to look anything up. A stamp that says 'I already sent this' keeps a copy from going around in circles.

sections.title: Traffic Class and Priority Objects
sections.content:
IEEE 802.1p lets frames carry a user_priority value that switches can use to tell traffic classes apart. IEEE makes no recommendation about how to use it, so the companion RFC 2815 provides the mappings. In SBM, a TCLASS object carries that value in a 3-bit field.

The flow of the TCLASS object is:

  • A DSBM MAY add a TCLASS object to a PATH that lacks one, using its own service mappings.
  • The Layer 3 device that receives the PATH removes and stores the object. When it later sends a RESV it must include the same object, and the original sender must then use that user_priority to override its own choice for marking outgoing packets.
  • A DSBM or SBM that cannot support the requested class may change it to a semantically lower value.
  • A DSBM client that accepts a RESV with a TCLASS and passes local admission control must give the value to its packet classifier.

Merging is strict. If a second RESV for an already admitted flow carries a different TCLASS from the installed one, the DSBM must send a RESV_ERR to the sender of the newer RESV with RSVP error code 21 (traffic control error) and sub-code 01.
sections.plainLanguage: The DSBM hands each rider a colored wristband that says which line they are in. The rider must wear it so the guards in every hallway can see where to send them.

sections.title: Electing the Designated SBM
sections.content:
Appendix A defines the election. A new SBM starts in DetectDSBM, listening for an existing DSBM. If it hears an I_AM_DSBM advertisement it goes to Idle. Otherwise it announces itself with a DSBM_WILLING message and enters ElectDSBM, where it resends the message every RefreshInterval. When the election timer fires, the best candidate seen declares itself with I_AM_DSBM and moves to IAMDSBM.

The best candidate has the highest SBM priority, an 8-bit value from 0 to 255. Ties go to the higher IP address. Priority 0 means not eligible. The RFC reserves ranges by device type: 128 to 255 for Layer 2 devices, 64 to 127 for routers and 1 to 63 for hosts.

The DSBM keeps sending I_AM_DSBM every RefreshInterval. Idle SBMs restart a dead-interval timer on each advertisement, and if it fires they start a new election. A DSBM shutting down sends DSBM_WILLING with priority set to zero. The suggested timer values are a RefreshInterval of about 5 seconds and a DSBMDeadInterval of 15 seconds (K=3 times the refresh), assuming RSVP uses 30 second refreshes. If no DSBM is present, a client may use ordinary RSVP forwarding.

Elections are scoped to a segment. Switches with SBM do not forward AllSBMAddress frames, so each segment elects its own DSBM. On a full-duplex link, one or two DSBMs may exist, one per direction.
sections.plainLanguage: Kids in a group pick a captain by comparing numbers on their badges. The captain calls out 'I am here' every few seconds, and if the calls stop, they vote again.

sections.title: Messages and Objects
sections.content:
Everything is built from RSVP messages with raw IP encapsulation and RSVP object formats. Two new message types are added: DSBM_WILLING (66) and I_AM_DSBM (67). Each message occupies one IP datagram. The new object classes carry the L2 and loopback information, the DSBM identity and its timers. The first three SBM-specific classes (RSVP_HOP_L2, LAN_NHOP and LAN_LOOPBACK) are chosen from the 10XXXXXX codespace, so RSVP nodes that do not know SBM ignore them without forwarding or raising an error.

L2 addresses are encoded as six octets in IEEE canonical format. An I_AM_DSBM message may also carry an optional NON_RESV_SEND_LIMIT object, a per-flow traffic profile (the Intserv SENDER_TSPEC parameters r, b, p, m and M) that a sender may use without a reservation. Hosts compare their flow to it. Absent the object, senders treat the limit as infinite. The RFC's example is that a 10 Mbps Ethernet with 10 hosts might allow a 16 Kbps telephony stream but not a 3 Mbps video stream. An administrator can forbid all unreserved traffic by setting r, b, p and M to 0.
sections.plainLanguage: The new messages are just notes written on the same paper RSVP already uses, with a few extra boxes. Old readers skip the boxes they do not understand.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says the message formatting and usage rules raise the same security issues as RSVP and Integrated Services. Access to enhanced qualities of service must be controlled and authenticated, as discussed in RFC 2205, RFC 2211 and RFC 2212.

An SBM implementation should satisfy the integrity requirements of RFC 2747 (RSVP Cryptographic Authentication), as for any RSVP implementation, and use the same mechanisms to protect the extra SBM objects. DSBM candidates should also be authenticated during the election, and a mechanism based on a shared secret among the candidates may be used, again following RFC 2747.
sections.plainLanguage: Only people with a real ticket should get to cut the line, and the hall monitors should check each other's badges so nobody can pretend to be the monitor.

items.label: DSBM_WILLING
items.desc: Message type: a candidate announces it would like to be the DSBM.

items.label: I_AM_DSBM
items.desc: Message type: the DSBM advertises itself every refresh interval.

items.label: RSVP_HOP_L2
items.desc: MAC address of the previous hop Layer 3 device.

items.label: LAN_NHOP_L2
items.desc: MAC address of the next hop Layer 3 device.

items.label: LAN_NHOP_L3
items.desc: IP address of the next hop Layer 3 device (IPv4 or IPv6).

items.label: LAN_LOOPBACK
items.desc: IP address of the outgoing interface, used to spot looped PATH messages.

items.label: DSBM IP ADDRESS
items.desc: IP address of the DSBM or candidate.

items.label: SBM_PRIORITY
items.desc: Priority used to choose among candidates.

items.label: DSBM Timer Intervals
items.desc: DeadInterval and RefreshInterval, each 0 to 255 seconds.

items.label: NON_RESV_SEND_LIMIT
items.desc: Optional limit on traffic a sender may send without a reservation.
